method: scripts/ib-research/claim-check.js: the passage is copied verbatim from the live source text at the pinned revision; VERIFIED = every claim number in one sentence that shares >= 50% of the claim's content words

records.claim: By mole fraction, dry air contains 78.08% nitrogen and 20.95% oxygen.
records.passage: By mole fraction (i.e., by quantity of molecules), dry air contains 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide, and small amounts of other trace gases (see Composition below for more detail).

records.claim: Carboniferous oxygen levels rose from low levels at the beginning of the period to highs of 25–30%.
records.passage: However, whilst exact numbers vary, all models show an overall increase in atmospheric oxygen levels from a low of between 15 and 20% at the beginning of the Carboniferous to highs of 25–30% during the Period.

records.claim: Meganeura had a single wing length reaching 32 centimetres and a wingspan around 65–75 cm.
records.passage: With a single-wing length of 32 centimetres (13 in), a wingspan about 65–75 cm (2.13–2.46 ft), and an estimated body length of up to 60–75 cm (1.97–2.46 ft), Meganeura monyi is one of the largest-known flying insect species, five times the length and twice the thoracic width of the largest modern dragonflies.

records.claim: In 1911 Édouard Harlé proposed that Meganeura could fly only because the atmosphere then contained more oxygen.
records.passage: Railway engineer Édouard Harlé originally proposed in 1911 that Meganeura was able to fly only because the atmosphere of Earth at that time contained more oxygen than the current 20%.

narration.text: Double Earth's oxygen, and fire changes first.
Today, dry air is about 20.95% oxygen.
With twice that, fires would start easier and spread faster.
In the Carboniferous, oxygen reached highs of 25 to 30%.
Dragonflies like Meganeura spanned up to 75 centimetres.
Doubling today's air goes far beyond even that world.
Giant insects would take many generations to evolve, if ever.
So the first thing you'd notice is fire, not bugs.
